title: The Karaites
hook: a movement that rejected the oral law and was argued with for centuries

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cairo geniza, a room that kept a world because nothing holy was thrown away. Your line was nothing holy thrown away. Today, a disagreement you could find in those very papers.

Friday evening, just before the Sabbath. In one Jewish home, the candles are lit, and they'll burn through the evening, giving light to the meal. In another Jewish home, a Karaite home of an earlier age, the lamps go out before the Sabbath begins, and the family keeps the holy day in the dark. Both homes read the same verse of the Torah, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Same verse. Both families Jewish. Two very different Friday nights, and the difference comes down to one question: is the written Torah enough on its own?
screen: `FRIDAY EVENING, TWO HOMES.` → `CANDLES BURNING, OR THE DARK.` → `IS THE WRITTEN TORAH ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: The Karaites are Jews who hold that the written Torah, the scripture itself, is the authority, and who do not accept the oral law of the Mishnah and Talmud as binding. Their name is usually explained from mikra, a Hebrew word for scripture, the text that is read. Tradition names Anan ben David as an early leader of the movement in Babylonia, and it grew in the lands we met this week. Back to the verse. The rabbinic tradition, the Rabbanites, reads it with the oral law: you may not kindle a fire on the Sabbath, but a light lit beforehand may keep burning. So, Sabbath candles. Karaite teachers, reading the verse on its own, took it to mean no fire may burn in the home on the Sabbath, even one lit before; Karaite practice today varies. Both sides were reading closely. They just started from different places. And they argued, for centuries. Saadia Gaon wrote against Karaite views, and Karaite scholars wrote back. The argument made both sides read harder: rely on scripture alone, and you need its Hebrew exactly; defend the oral law, and you have to show how it fits the written words. The book of Proverbs says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "Iron sharpeneth iron," and the Talmud applies that verse to scholars who sharpen each other in study. Karaite communities still exist today, keeping their own way.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group whose way of doing things differs from yours, in faith, politics, family habits, anything. Ask what text, value or experience they start from, and find one thing they're trying to protect that you might care about too; you don't have to agree, just see where they're standing. If you pray, you can ask for a fair mind.
